note: Network-wide attack methodology. Original content, methodology level. The tool prints this reference; it never executes any of it. Run only against systems you are authorised to test.

topics.name: Sniffing & ARP spoofing (MITM)
topics.summary: On a switched LAN, poison the ARP caches of a victim and the gateway so traffic routes through you, then read or alter it. The base layer-2 man-in-the-middle that most other LAN attacks build on.
topics.applies_when: You have a foothold on the same broadcast domain (a LAN port, a wireless client, a compromised host) and no dynamic ARP inspection is enforced.

rows.expect: Cleartext credentials and tokens for any unencrypted protocol sharing the segment (FTP, HTTP, SNMP, LDAP simple bind).
rows.mitigation: Encrypt everything in transit; segment the network; use switch port security.

rows.command: bettercap -iface eth0 -eval "set arp.spoof.targets <victim>; arp.spoof on; net.sniff on"
rows.expect: Victim and gateway send their traffic to you; you relay it and capture or modify it in flight.
rows.mitigation: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) with DHCP snooping; use static ARP for critical hosts.

rows.expect: Strips or downgrades TLS on victims that allow it, exposing session content.
rows.mitigation: Enforce HSTS with preload; pin certificates; HTTPS-only.

topics.name: LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS / WPAD poisoning & NTLM relay
topics.summary: Windows falls back to broadcast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) and to WPAD proxy auto-discovery when DNS fails. Answer those broadcasts to capture NetNTLM hashes, or relay the authentication to another host for code execution without ever cracking it.
topics.applies_when: A Windows network where LLMNR/NBT-NS are still enabled and SMB signing is not required on at least some hosts.

rows.expect: NetNTLMv1/v2 hashes from hosts that mistype a share or hostname; crack offline with hashcat mode 5600.
rows.mitigation: Disable LLMNR (GPO) and NBT-NS; disable WPAD; require SMB signing.

rows.expect: Authentication relayed to targets without SMB signing: command execution, SAM dump, or a session as the captured user.
rows.mitigation: Enforce SMB signing everywhere; enable EPA/channel binding on LDAP and HTTP.

rows.expect: Browsers requesting wpad.dat prompt for and leak domain credentials to a rogue proxy.
rows.mitigation: Create a real wpad DNS record (or disable auto-proxy); disable Web Proxy Auto-Discovery.

topics.name: DHCPv6 spoofing & IPv6 DNS takeover (mitm6)
topics.summary: Even IPv4-only networks usually leave IPv6 on. Answer the clients' DHCPv6 solicitations to assign yourself as their IPv6 DNS server, then route name resolution (and WPAD) through you — a reliable primary vector into Active Directory.
topics.applies_when: Windows clients with IPv6 enabled (the default) on a segment where no DHCPv6 guard is configured.

rows.expect: Clients accept you as their DNS server over IPv6 and send you their queries, including WPAD.
rows.mitigation: Enable RA Guard and DHCPv6 Guard on switches; disable IPv6 if genuinely unused; block rogue RAs.

rows.expect: Relayed LDAP authentication can create a computer account or grant delegation, leading to privilege escalation in AD.
rows.mitigation: Require LDAP channel binding and signing; restrict who can add computer accounts (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 0).

topics.name: Pentesting IPv6
topics.summary: IPv6 is frequently unmonitored. Discover live IPv6 hosts via multicast and neighbour discovery, then scan them directly — they often expose the same services as IPv4 with none of the firewalling.
topics.applies_when: Any segment where IPv6 is active; especially dual-stack hosts whose IPv6 interface is less protected than IPv4.

rows.expect: A list of responding IPv6 hosts on the link, including ones with no IPv4 service exposed.
rows.mitigation: Apply equivalent firewall policy to IPv6; monitor ICMPv6; RA Guard.

rows.expect: Neighbour cache entries mapping IPv6 addresses to MACs for follow-up scanning.
rows.mitigation: Segment IPv6; restrict neighbour discovery; monitor NDP.

rows.expect: Open services on the IPv6 interface, often unfiltered compared to the IPv4 side of the same host.
rows.mitigation: Firewall IPv6 to parity with IPv4; disable unused IPv6.

topics.name: VLAN hopping / lateral segmentation bypass
topics.summary: Reach VLANs you were not placed in, either by negotiating a trunk with a switch that leaves DTP on (switch spoofing) or by double-tagging frames so the first tag is stripped and the second delivers you into another VLAN.
topics.applies_when: An access port with DTP enabled, or a native-VLAN misconfiguration that allows double-tagged frames to leak.

rows.command: yersinia -I   # enable trunking via DTP, then read 802.1Q tags
rows.expect: The port becomes a trunk and you receive traffic for every VLAN; create sub-interfaces per tag to reach them.
rows.mitigation: Disable DTP (switchport nonegotiate); set access ports to 'switchport mode access'.

rows.expect: A one-way frame is delivered into the target VLAN when the native VLAN matches the outer tag.
rows.mitigation: Never use VLAN 1 as native; set a dedicated unused native VLAN; prune trunks.

topics.name: GLBP & HSRP (first-hop redundancy) attacks
topics.summary: HSRP, VRRP and GLBP elect a virtual default gateway by priority. If the election packets are unauthenticated (or use the well-known cleartext key), claim the highest priority to become the active gateway and route the segment's traffic through you.
topics.applies_when: You can see HSRP/VRRP/GLBP hellos on the segment and they carry no authentication or a default/cleartext key.

rows.command: wireshark -i eth0 -f 'proto 112 or udp port 1985 or udp port 3222'
rows.expect: Group, virtual IP, current priority and any authentication in the HSRP/VRRP/GLBP hellos.
rows.mitigation: Authenticate FHRP with a strong key; restrict which ports may source the protocol.

rows.command: loki_gtk.py   # send HSRP coup with priority 255
rows.expect: You become the active gateway; victims route through you, giving a full man-in-the-middle for the subnet.
rows.mitigation: Use the maximum priority on real routers plus MD5 auth; enable port security.

topics.name: EIGRP attacks
topics.summary: EIGRP forms neighbour adjacencies and exchanges routes. Where it is unauthenticated, inject yourself as a neighbour to advertise bogus routes (blackhole or redirect traffic) or flood the process.
topics.applies_when: You observe EIGRP hellos (IP protocol 88, multicast 224.0.0.10) with no MD5/SHA authentication.

rows.expect: EIGRP hellos revealing the autonomous-system number and whether authentication is set.
rows.mitigation: Enable EIGRP authentication (key-chain); use passive-interface on access segments.

rows.command: # craft an EIGRP neighbour with Scapy and advertise a /0 route
rows.expect: Traffic for the advertised prefixes is pulled toward you — a redirect or blackhole.
rows.mitigation: Authenticate the routing protocol; filter routes; restrict adjacencies to known interfaces.

topics.name: IDS / IPS evasion
topics.summary: Signature and reassembly engines can be slipped with fragmentation, decoys, timing and source manipulation. Useful to confirm whether a negative scan result reflects a hardened host or a sensor dropping your probes.
topics.applies_when: A scan returns suspiciously little, or you need to test whether network sensors detect the assessment traffic.

rows.expect: Fragmented packets that may pass sensors doing no reassembly.
rows.mitigation: Enforce full stream reassembly on the IPS; drop tiny fragments.

rows.expect: Your real source address is hidden among decoys in the logs.
rows.mitigation: Correlate on behaviour, not single source IPs; rate-limit.

rows.expect: Probe rate below threshold-based detection windows.
rows.mitigation: Use long-baseline anomaly detection, not just short-window thresholds.

rows.expect: Probes sourced from a trusted port (53, 88) may bypass weak ACLs.
rows.mitigation: Do not trust source ports in firewall rules; use stateful policy.

topics.name: SSDP & UPnP spoofing (EvilSSDP)
topics.summary: Hosts discover services by multicasting SSDP searches. Answer them with a rogue device whose description points at an attacker page to phish credentials or deliver content, or abuse writable UPnP IGD rules.
topics.applies_when: SSDP (UDP 1900) is open on the segment and clients browse network devices.

rows.expect: Victims browsing network devices open your fake device page; a credential template harvests logins.
rows.mitigation: Disable UPnP/SSDP where not needed; filter multicast 1900; user awareness.

rows.expect: The internet gateway's port-mapping table; writable mappings can expose internal hosts.
rows.mitigation: Disable UPnP IGD on gateways; restrict port-mapping to trusted clients.

topics.name: DDS / RTPS service impersonation
topics.summary: DDS (Data Distribution Service) over RTPS is used in robotics, ROS 2 and industrial systems. Unauthenticated participants can be discovered and impersonated to read or publish topic data.
topics.applies_when: You find RTPS discovery traffic (default UDP 7400+) on an OT/robotics segment with DDS security disabled.

rows.command: # capture RTPS discovery on UDP 7400-7500 and enumerate participants
rows.expect: The list of DDS participants, topics and data types on the bus.
rows.mitigation: Enable the DDS Security plugins (authentication, access control, encryption); segment OT networks.

rows.command: # join the domain and publish to a discovered topic
rows.expect: Injected data accepted by subscribers when no authentication is enforced.
rows.mitigation: Require mutual authentication and signed data; isolate the DDS domain.

rows.expect: Subscribers spend resources on fake participants, degrading the bus.
rows.mitigation: Rate-limit discovery; isolate the DDS domain; enable the DDS Security access-control plugin.

topics.name: Telecom network exploitation
topics.summary: Mobile core and interconnect protocols — GTP, SS7, Diameter, SIP — carry little inherent authentication. On a reachable core or roaming interface they allow subscriber tracking, interception and fraud. High-level reference; relevant only on telecom infrastructure.
topics.applies_when: The engagement scope includes a mobile core, a lab EPC, or an SS7/Diameter interconnect you are authorised to test.

rows.command: # probe GTP-C on UDP 2123 and enumerate reachable nodes
rows.expect: Reachable SGSN/GGSN/PGW endpoints and whether GTP is filtered at the edge.
rows.mitigation: Enforce GTP firewalling at borders (GRX/IPX); validate TEIDs; rate-limit.

rows.command: # issue MAP/Diameter queries against an authorised test core
rows.expect: Subscriber location or interception where the signalling link trusts the peer.
rows.mitigation: Deploy SS7/Diameter firewalls; apply GSMA FS.11/FS.19 category filtering; monitor for cross-category messages.

rows.command: svmap <range>   # then svwar to enumerate extensions
rows.expect: Reachable SIP devices and valid extensions for follow-up.
rows.mitigation: Authenticate SIP; restrict signalling to trusted peers; rate-limit REGISTER/INVITE.

topics.name: WebRTC DoS
topics.summary: WebRTC's STUN/TURN and media paths can be abused for amplification and resource exhaustion against clients or relays, or to reveal a target's real IP behind a proxy via ICE candidates.
topics.applies_when: A target application uses WebRTC (video/voice, conferencing) and you are assessing its availability or privacy exposure.

rows.command: # collect ICE candidates from the offer/answer exchange
rows.expect: Host and server-reflexive candidates can reveal a client's real address behind a VPN or proxy.
rows.mitigation: Force relay-only ICE (TURN) for sensitive deployments; filter host candidates.

rows.command: # flood allocation/binding requests at the TURN server
rows.expect: Degraded or exhausted relay capacity, denying service to legitimate sessions.
rows.mitigation: Authenticate TURN (long-term credentials); rate-limit allocations; quota per user.

rows.command: # modify the SDP offer/answer in the signalling channel
rows.expect: Forced codec or candidate changes that break or redirect the media session.
rows.mitigation: Authenticate and integrity-protect signalling (DTLS-SRTP, secure WebSocket).

reference.name: Network protocols explained
reference.summary: Short reference for the layer-2/3 protocols the attacks above target, so the technique and its fix make sense in context.

rows.expect: Maps IPv4 to MAC with no authentication — the basis of LAN MITM.
rows.mitigation: Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping.

rows.expect: IPv6's neighbour and router discovery; rogue RAs redirect traffic.
rows.mitigation: RA Guard, DHCPv6 Guard.

rows.mitigation: Disable via GPO; rely on DNS only.
